title: Fashion Business Management: Production Operations for Scaling
subtitle: Turn a busy tailoring practice into a managed workroom with timed operations, minute costing, quality gates and a 90-day growth plan.
description: An advanced, hands-on course for fashion business owners who already sew and sell. You measure where your hours go, standardise your styles with operation sheets and golden samples, run a job board with WIP limits and quality gates, cost garments by the minute, and grow through boutiques, contracts and a fairly paid team.
outcomes: Run a time audit and order-mix review to find the constraint in your workroom
Write operation sheets with timed standard minutes and keep golden samples
Run a one-page SOP and job board with WIP limits, quality gates and a defect log
Build a minute-based costing sheet for your three most-ordered garments and calculate monthly capacity
Test wholesale, consignment, contract and CMT offers on cost, cash and capacity
Set fair pay and write a 90-day growth plan with a monthly dashboard
audience: Women who already run a tailoring or fashion business with at least one helper and want to produce more, to a steady standard, without sewing every piece themselves.
tools: Smartphone with a stopwatch and calculator
Notebook or ticket book for job tickets and logs
A wall or large paper for the job board, or a free board app such as Trello
Measuring tape and your current patterns and samples
WhatsApp Business for client and buyer messages

modules.title: From Maker to Manager: Diagnosing and Standardising Your Workroom
modules.overview: You audit where your hours go, choose a production model mix with numbers, and turn your personal standard into operation sheets, timed standards and a golden sample that others can learn from.

lessons.title: Where your hours go: the owner time audit and the order-mix review
objectives: Run a two-week time log of your own working hours by task
Separate owner-only tasks from tasks a trained person could do
Calculate fee income per owner hour for each type of order you take
Name the one constraint that stops your workroom from taking more work

blocks.text: This course is about **production operations**: how a fashion business that already has paying clients turns into a workroom that can produce more garments, at a known cost, to a steady standard, without the owner sewing every seam. It assumes you can already cut, sew and price a garment. If you still need those basics, take the Fashion Business Management core course and the tailoring courses first, then come back here.

Every scale-up starts with one honest question: **where do my hours actually go?** Most owners guess, and most guesses are wrong. You may feel you spend your day sewing, but when you write it down you find that buying trims at the market, answering WhatsApp messages and redoing other people's work eat a large share of the week. You cannot plan capacity, hire well or set targets until you know this.

blocks.name: time-management
blocks.alt: A woman checking a large clock beside a task list
blocks.caption: The first scale-up tool is a simple log of where each working hour went.

blocks.text: Step one: the two-week time log

For ten working days, keep a log in a notebook or a note on your phone. Every time you switch task, write the time and the task. Do not judge or tidy it, just record. At the end of each day, add up the hours under a few fixed headings. Use the same headings every day so you can total them later.

items: **Cutting**: laying out fabric, marking, cutting pieces
**Sewing**: all machine work
**Finishing**: hand stitches, buttons, pressing
**Client time**: consultations, measuring, fittings, collections
**Buying**: trips to the market for fabric, linings, zips, thread
**Admin and messages**: WhatsApp replies, records, chasing payments
**Rework**: unpicking and correcting faults, yours or a helper's

blocks.text: Two weeks is the minimum because one week can be unusual, for example a week with a big wedding delivery. If you have helpers, ask them to log too. Their logs show where they wait for you, which is often the biggest hidden cost in a growing workroom.
Step two: sort owner-only work from transferable work

Look at each heading and ask: **could a trained person do this to my standard, with a written method and a check?** Cutting a complex lace gown for a bride may truly need you for now. Overlocking seams, sewing straight side seams, pressing, buying standard trims from a list and replying to price questions with a ready message usually do not. Mark each heading as owner-only or transferable. Be strict: "they will not do it as well as me" is often true at first, but it is a training problem, not a reason to keep the task forever.

blocks.title: Worked example: Adaeze's two-week log
blocks.context: Adaeze (for example) runs a three-machine workroom in Ibadan with two helpers. She logged 120 working hours over ten days.
steps: Totals: cutting 30 h, sewing 34 h, finishing 10 h, client time 18 h, buying 12 h, admin and messages 16 h. Check: 30 + 34 + 10 + 18 + 12 + 16 = 120 h.
She marks cutting and client time as owner-only for now: 30 + 18 = 48 h, which is 48 ÷ 120 = 40% of her time.
Sewing, finishing, buying and admin are transferable: 34 + 10 + 12 + 16 = 72 h, which is 60% of her time.
Her helpers' logs show they waited for her to cut pieces on most mornings.
blocks.result: Six of every ten hours Adaeze works could be done by someone else. Her real bottleneck is cutting: helpers sit idle until she cuts. Her first scale-up move is to free cutting time, not to buy another machine.

blocks.text: Step three: the order-mix review

Now look at the last three months of orders in your order book. Group them by type, for example aso-ebi pieces, one-off bespoke outfits, alterations, ready-made items. For each type, write the number of orders, the income, and a fair estimate of owner hours per order. Divide income by owner hours. This gives **income per owner hour**, the number that tells you which work feeds the business and which work only keeps you busy.

In this illustrative example, bespoke outfits bring in the most money, but aso-ebi pieces pay more for each hour of Adaeze's time, because the same style is repeated across a group and she cuts several at once. Alterations pay least per hour. That does not mean she must stop alterations; they bring new clients. It means alterations are a good first task to hand to a trained helper.

blocks.title: Which work to keep, grow or hand over
items: Grow: high value, transferable
Keep for now: high value, owner-only
Hand over first: low value, transferable
Reprice or drop: low value, owner-only
axes: Needs the owner (left: no, right: yes)
blocks.caption: Place each order type in a box: the left column is where scaling happens, because others can do that work.

blocks.text: Find your one constraint

A workroom moves at the speed of its slowest step. In operations language this is the **constraint** or **bottleneck**. It may be the owner's cutting time, one overlocker shared by three machinists, the time it takes to get to the market, or clients who arrive late for fittings. Adding machines before you fix the constraint simply adds more idle machines. Write one sentence: "Right now my workroom is limited by ____." Every module in this course gives you tools to widen that point.

blocks.title: Record honestly, not proudly
blocks.text: Log the hours you spend on your phone too. Many owners find that one or two hours a day go to WhatsApp chats that could be answered with saved quick replies in WhatsApp Business. Honest data gives you a plan that works.

takeaways: Scaling starts with facts about your own hours, not with buying machines
Split tasks into owner-only and transferable, and be strict
Income per owner hour shows which orders really feed the business
Find the single constraint and widen it before adding capacity elsewhere

activity.title: Your two-week time audit
steps: Set up a log with the seven headings from this lesson
Record every task switch for ten working days
Total each heading and mark it owner-only or transferable
Group three months of orders by type and calculate income per owner hour
Write one sentence naming your current constraint
activity.evidence: A photo of your completed log totals and your order-mix table with the constraint sentence underneath

lessons.title: Choosing your production model mix: bespoke, made-to-measure, batch ready-to-wear and CMT
objectives: Describe four production models and how each one earns money
Compare models using contribution per workroom hour
Check three readiness signs before moving work into batches
Choose a model mix that suits your skills, cash and clients

blocks.text: A fashion business can make the same skill pay in very different ways. The way you take orders and organise sewing is your **production model**. Most Nigerian workrooms start fully bespoke. Scaling usually means adding one or two other models alongside it, so that some work becomes repeatable. This lesson compares four models and shows how to judge them with numbers, not feelings.

blocks.name: dress
blocks.caption: The same dress style can be sold as a bespoke piece, a made-to-measure order or a ready-made batch.

blocks.text: The four models

head: Model
How it works
Who buys fabric
Main risk
rows: One client, one pattern drafted to her body, several fittings
Owner time per piece is high; hard to delegate
Your tested standard pattern, adjusted to the client's measurements, one fitting
Needs good standard blocks and measurement discipline
You make a run of one style in set sizes and sell from stock
Cash tied up in stock; unsold sizes
Another brand gives you fabric and a sample; you cut, sew and finish for a fee per piece
Low fee per piece; you must hit their standard and deadline

blocks.text: Bespoke builds reputation and suits weddings and special events. Made-to-measure is the bridge to scale: the client still gets a fitted garment, but you cut from a proven pattern, so a trained helper can do most of the work. Batch RTW lets you cut many layers at once and sew in a line, which is where production speed comes from. CMT fills idle machine time with work that needs no selling, which is why many growing workrooms take it in quiet months.
Judging a model: contribution per workroom hour

**Contribution** is the selling price minus the materials and other costs that rise with each piece. It is the money left to pay wages, rent and you. Divide it by the workroom hours each piece takes and you get **contribution per workroom hour**. Because hours are the thing you run out of, this number compares models fairly. Include the hit from unsold stock for RTW, because a top that never sells has used materials and hours but earned nothing.

blocks.title: Worked example: four models, one workroom
blocks.context: Adaeze (for example) compares four kinds of job. All prices are approximate and for illustration.
steps: Bespoke lace gown: price ₦120,000, materials ₦55,000, 14 workroom hours. Contribution ₦65,000 ÷ 14 = about ₦4,643 per hour.
Made-to-measure corporate dress from her standard block: price ₦38,000, materials ₦14,000, 4 hours. Contribution ₦24,000 ÷ 4 = ₦6,000 per hour.

Batch of 20 peplum tops: price ₦15,000 each, materials ₦5,200 each, 1.6 hours each, so 32 hours. If only 14 sell in the season: income 14 × ₦15,000 = ₦210,000, materials 20 × ₦5,200 = ₦104,000, contribution ₦106,000 ÷ 32 = about ₦3,313 per hour. If all 20 sell it is ₦6,125 per hour.
CMT shirts for another brand: fee ₦4,500 each, her thread and labels ₦400, 1.1 hours each. Contribution ₦4,100 ÷ 1.1 = about ₦3,727 per hour.
blocks.result: Made-to-measure gives Adaeze the best and safest return per hour. Batch RTW only beats it when nearly every piece sells, so she starts with small runs. CMT pays less per hour but needs no selling, so she uses it to fill gaps, not as her main line.

blocks.title: Made for one versus made for many
items: Bespoke and made-to-measure
Batch RTW and CMT
left: Owner time per piece is high
blocks.caption: Most scaling workrooms run a mix: personal work for reputation, batch work for volume.

blocks.text: Three readiness signs before you batch

items: **Consistency**: two different people in your workroom can make the same style to the same measurements and finish. Test it by giving the same cut pieces to two helpers and comparing.
**Known cost**: you know the true cost of each style, including fabric waste, trims, labour minutes and overhead (Module 2 builds this).
**Cash cover**: you can buy fabric for a batch and wait for sales without missing rent or wages. If not, start with pre-orders or CMT, where the client funds materials.

blocks.text: If one sign is missing, fix it first. Moving into batches without consistency simply multiplies your faults by twenty. Moving without cash cover is how many workrooms end up with a shelf of unsold stock and no money for the next order.
Choosing your mix

items: List the models you use now and the share of income each brings.
Calculate contribution per workroom hour for one typical job in each model.
Check the three readiness signs honestly.
Choose a target mix for the next three months, for example 50% made-to-measure, 30% bespoke, 20% CMT in quiet weeks.
Decide what you will stop or reprice, such as one-off styles that take many hours for a low fee.

blocks.title: Protect your cash with CMT and batch work
blocks.text: For CMT, agree in writing the fee per piece, the quantity, who pays for spoiled fabric, the delivery date and when you are paid. For RTW, start with a small run in your best-selling sizes and take pre-orders on WhatsApp before cutting more.

takeaways: Bespoke, made-to-measure, batch RTW and CMT each earn in a different way
Compare models by contribution per workroom hour, including unsold stock
Made-to-measure is often the best bridge from bespoke to scale
Check consistency, known cost and cash cover before you batch

activity.title: Compare your models
steps: Pick one recent job from each model you use or could use
Write price, materials and workroom hours for each
Calculate contribution per workroom hour, checking the sums with a calculator
Score yourself on the three readiness signs
Write your target model mix for the next three months
activity.evidence: A one-page sheet with your four calculations, readiness scores and chosen mix

lessons.title: Making your standard teachable: operation breakdowns, timed standard minutes and the golden sample
objectives: Break a garment into a numbered list of sewing operations
Time an operation and turn it into a standard minute value
Keep an approved golden sample with its specification card
Train a helper with a four-stage show-and-sign-off ladder

blocks.text: When you are the only maker, the standard lives in your hands and head. To scale, the standard must live on paper and in a reference garment, so that anyone you train can reach it. Garment factories do this with three tools: an **operation breakdown**, a **standard time for each operation**, and an **approved sample**. You can use the same tools in a three-machine workroom.

blocks.name: teaching
blocks.alt: A woman explaining steps on a board to a learner
blocks.caption: Leaders in a workroom transfer skill with written steps, timed targets and a sample to compare against.

blocks.text: The operation breakdown

An **operation** is one task a person does from start to finish at one station, for example "sew both bust darts" or "insert invisible zip". Write every operation for a style in the order the garment is built. Number them. Keep each one small enough that a new helper can learn it in a day or two. This list becomes your training plan, your production plan and the base of your costing.
Timing an operation: from observed time to standard minutes

A **standard minute value (SMV)** is the time a trained worker should need for an operation at a normal pace, including small allowances. Work-study practice builds it in three steps: time the task to get the **observed time**, adjust it for how fast the person worked compared with a normal pace (the **rating**), then add an **allowance** for fatigue, personal needs and small delays.

items: Choose a trained worker and explain you are timing the task, not judging her.
Use your phone stopwatch. Time the same operation at least five times on real garments.
Average the times. This is the observed time.
Rate her pace: 100% means normal steady pace, 90% means a little slower, 110% a little faster. Multiply the observed time by the rating to get normal time.
Add an allowance, for example 15%, by multiplying by 1.15. Write the result as the standard minutes for that operation.

blocks.title: Worked example: timing an invisible zip
blocks.context: Adaeze (for example) times her helper Chioma inserting invisible zips on shift dresses.
steps: Five timings in minutes: 9.5, 10.2, 9.8, 10.5, 10.0. Total 50.0, so observed time = 50.0 ÷ 5 = 10.0 minutes.
Chioma is careful but a little slow, so Adaeze rates her at 90%. Normal time = 10.0 × 0.90 = 9.0 minutes.
Adaeze adds a 15% allowance: 9.0 × 1.15 = 10.35 minutes.
She rounds to 10 minutes for planning and writes it on the operation sheet.
blocks.result: The zip operation has a standard of about 10 minutes. If a trained helper regularly takes 20, she needs coaching or the method needs fixing.

head: No.
Operation: sleeveless shift dress
Standard minutes (example)
rows: Cut pieces from the lay (per garment)
Hand finishing: hook and eye, tack facings
Total standard minutes for the dress

blocks.text: The total, 75 minutes in this example, is the dress's **SMV**. Your numbers will be different; time your own team. Once you have an SMV for each style, you can plan how many pieces a day the workroom can make and what labour each piece really costs. You will use these numbers in Module 2.
The golden sample and specification card

A **golden sample** is one garment of each style that you have checked and approved as the standard. Label it with the style code, size, date and your signature, and keep it clean in a bag, not on the rail for sale. With it, keep a **specification card**: a photo or sketch, key finished measurements, seam allowances, stitch type and length, thread colour, trims list and the operation list. When a helper asks "is this right?", the answer is "compare it with the golden sample", not "ask madam".

blocks.title: The training ladder for each operation
items: I show, you watch
We do it together
You do, I check
Signed off on chart
blocks.caption: A helper climbs the ladder one operation at a time and is signed off only when three pieces in a row match the sample.

blocks.text: Leading the training

items: Train one operation at a time, starting with the simplest, such as overlocking edges or pressing.
Give practice pieces from offcuts before real client fabric.
Sign off an operation when the helper makes three pieces in a row that match the golden sample within the standard time plus a margin you choose for learners.
Keep a wall chart: names down the side, operation numbers across the top, a tick when signed off. It shows at a glance who can cover whom.

blocks.title: Train safe habits with every operation
blocks.text: Show the safe way first: fingers clear of the needle, machine switched off before changing needles or threading, scissors and rotary cutters closed and placed down, irons stood on their heel and switched off at the wall when not in use. A fast operation done unsafely is not signed off.

takeaways: Write each style as a numbered list of small operations
Standard minutes come from observed time, a pace rating and an allowance
A labelled golden sample and spec card hold the standard, not your memory
Sign off operations only after three matching pieces in a row

activity.title: Build one style's operation sheet
steps: Choose your most-ordered style
Write its operations in build order
Time at least three operations five times each and calculate standard minutes
Approve and label a golden sample with a specification card
Start a training wall chart with your helpers' names
activity.evidence: A photo of the operation sheet with timings, the labelled golden sample and the wall chart

quiz.q: Adaeze logs 120 hours. Cutting 30 h and client time 18 h are owner-only. What share of her time is transferable?
quiz.explain: Owner-only is 30 + 18 = 48 h, which is 40%. The rest, 72 h out of 120, is 60% transferable.

quiz.q: Her helpers wait each morning until she cuts. What is the best first scale-up move?
options: Free up or delegate cutting time, for example by training a cutter
Lower her prices to get more clients
quiz.explain: Cutting is the constraint. Adding machines adds idle capacity; widening the bottleneck lets the whole workroom move faster.

quiz.q: A batch of 20 tops uses ₦104,000 of materials and 32 hours. Only 14 sell at ₦15,000. What is contribution per workroom hour?
Which sign shows a workroom is NOT yet ready to move a style into batch production?
options: Two helpers made the same style to the same measurements
She knows the full cost of the style
Each helper finishes the style differently and she corrects them all
She has cash to buy fabric for a small run
quiz.explain: Batching without consistency multiplies faults. Consistency must be fixed first.

quiz.q: A worker's average observed time is 8.0 minutes, her pace is rated 110%, and the allowance is 15%. What is the standard time?
What is the main purpose of a golden sample?
options: To sell at a premium price
To act as the approved reference that every piece is compared against
To show clients the fabric colour
quiz.explain: The golden sample holds the standard so helpers can check their work without depending on the owner's memory.

modules.title: Running the Workroom: SOPs, Quality Gates, Costing and Capacity
modules.overview: You put every order on a job board with a one-page SOP and WIP limits, build quality checks into the line with a defect log, and cost garments by the minute so you know both your true price and your monthly capacity.

lessons.title: The workroom SOP and job board: tickets, stages and work-in-progress limits
objectives: Write a one-page SOP from intake to delivery with named stage owners
Set up a job ticket that travels with every garment
Run a visual job board with a limit on work in progress
Use Little's law to estimate how long garments spend in the workroom

blocks.text: A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** is the written way your workroom handles every order, so that the result does not depend on who is on duty or how busy the week is. In a fashion workroom the SOP covers the journey from intake to delivery. It should fit on one page and be stuck on the wall where everyone can see it.

blocks.name: scrum-board
blocks.alt: People moving cards across a board with columns
blocks.caption: A job board shows every garment's stage at a glance, so nothing hides in a pile.

blocks.text: The stages and their owners

head: Stage
What happens
Done when
Owner (example)
rows: Style agreed, measurements or size taken, fabric received and checked, deposit paid, due date set
Pattern chosen, fabric laid, pieces cut, notched and bundled with the ticket
Operations done in order from the operation sheet
Hand finishing, buttons, hooks, thread trimming, pressing
Checked against measurements and golden sample
Client told, balance collected, garment handed over or dispatched

blocks.text: Each stage has an owner and a clear **done when** rule. The rule stops arguments such as "I thought you had cut it". If a garment fails inspection, it goes back to the stage that caused the fault, and the ticket records why.
The job ticket

A **job ticket** is a small card or sheet that stays with the garment from cutting to delivery. Use a printed template or a ruled page in a ticket book. It carries: ticket number, client first name and phone, style code, size or measurement card number, fabric description, trims, due date, deposit and balance, a row for each stage with initials and date, and inspection result. Clip it to the cut bundle so it moves with the pieces. Keep client phone numbers only on the ticket and your order book, not on public boards.
The job board and WIP limits

A **job board** is a wall board or large paper divided into columns, one per stage. Each order is a sticky note or card with its ticket number and due date. When the garment moves, the card moves. If you prefer your phone, a free board app such as Trello works the same way, and WhatsApp Business labels can tag chats as New order, In progress or Ready.

The key rule comes from kanban, a scheduling method developed at Toyota: **limit work in progress (WIP)**. Decide the most cards allowed in each column, for example no more than 8 garments in Sew at once. When the column is full, nobody cuts more; the cutter helps finish instead. This feels slow at first, but it stops half-made garments piling up, and it shows you immediately where work is stuck.

blocks.title: One garment's path through the board
items: Intake and deposit
Cut and bundle
Sew operations
Finish and press
Inspect and sign
Deliver and close
blocks.caption: Cards move left to right; a full column is a signal to clear work before starting more.

blocks.text: How long do garments really take? Little's law

Little's law, widely used in manufacturing, links three numbers: **work in progress = throughput × lead time**. Turn it around and **average lead time = work in progress ÷ throughput**. Throughput is how many garments you finish per day. You do not need software: count the cards on your board each morning and count the garments delivered each day for two weeks, then average.

blocks.title: Worked example: why Adaeze's clients wait nine days
blocks.context: Adaeze (for example) counts her board every morning for two weeks.
steps: Average cards between Cut and Inspect: 36 garments.
Average garments finished per working day: 4.
Average time in the workroom = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 working days.

She wants 5 days. Option A: keep throughput at 4 a day and cut WIP to 4 × 5 = 20 garments, by not cutting new work until the Sew column drops. Option B: keep WIP at 36 and raise throughput to 36 ÷ 5 = 7.2 garments a day, which needs more people or hours.
blocks.result: Option A costs nothing. By capping WIP at 20, each garment spends about 5 days inside, clients get dates she can keep, and the same team delivers the same number per day.

blocks.text: Writing your one-page SOP

items: Write the six stages as headings down the page.
Under each, write three to five short action lines in the order they happen.
Add the done when rule and the owner's role.
Mark quality checkpoints with a star (Lesson 2 shows where).
Add your WIP limits per column and the rule for urgent orders, for example a maximum of two rush jobs a week at a rush fee.
Read it with your team, change anything unclear, then sign and date it.

blocks.title: Due dates are promises
blocks.text: Set the client's due date from your board, not from hope. Count the cards already in the workroom, use your lead time, and add a buffer of a few days for fittings. A date you keep builds more trust than a fast date you miss.

takeaways: A one-page SOP names each stage, its owner and its done when rule
A job ticket travels with every garment from cut to delivery
Limit work in progress per column to stop piles and reveal blockages
Average lead time equals work in progress divided by daily throughput

activity.title: Put your workroom on a board
steps: Draw a six-column job board on paper or set one up in an app
Write a card for every garment now in the workroom
Choose a WIP limit for the Sew column
Count cards and finished garments daily for one week and work out lead time
Draft your one-page SOP and read it with your team
activity.evidence: Photos of your job board and your signed one-page SOP, plus your lead-time calculation

lessons.title: Building quality into the line: in-process gates, a defect log and the cost of rework
objectives: Place four quality gates along the production flow
Keep a defect log and calculate a defect rate
Use a Pareto table to find the few faults causing most rework
Put a naira cost on rework and on safety and privacy lapses

blocks.text: Checking a garment only at the end catches faults when they are most expensive to fix: the hem is sewn, the zip is in, the facing is understitched. Production workrooms build quality **into the line** with short checks at each stage. Your Fashion Finishing course covers how to inspect a finished garment in detail; this lesson is about the system around it: where checks happen, how faults are counted and what they cost.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: A simple defect log on a clipboard turns complaints into numbers you can act on.

blocks.text: Four quality gates

blocks.title: Quality gates in a fashion workroom
items: Fabric and trims check
Cut check before sewing
First-piece check per operation
Final inspection before press
blocks.caption: Each gate stops a fault from travelling further down the line, where fixing it costs more.

items: **Fabric and trims check (intake)**: measure the fabric length, look along the whole piece in daylight for holes, shading and print faults, and check zips and buttons match the order. Note problems on the ticket before cutting.

**Cut check**: count pieces against the pattern list, check grain lines and notches, and match the size or measurement card. A cutting error found here costs minutes; found after sewing it can cost the fabric.
**First-piece check**: when a machinist starts an operation on a new style or batch, the first piece is compared with the golden sample before she continues.
**Final inspection**: measurements, symmetry, stitching, finishing and cleanliness, against the specification card, before the final press.

blocks.text: The defect log

Every time a gate finds a fault, write one line in the defect log: date, ticket number, operation, type of fault, who found it and the minutes spent fixing it. Keep fault names fixed, for example uneven hem, zip ripples, wrong size, loose threads, iron shine or stain, skipped stitches. At month end, the **defect rate** is the number of garments with at least one fault divided by the number inspected.
Pareto: fix the vital few first

Pareto analysis sorts causes from most to least frequent and adds a running cumulative percentage. Often a few fault types cause most of the rework, so you fix those first. The split is not always 80/20; it may be 70/30 or 90/10, but the method still shows where to aim.

blocks.title: Worked example: Adaeze's month of defects
blocks.context: Adaeze (for example) inspected 180 garments in a month. 27 had at least one fault.
steps: Defect rate = 27 ÷ 180 = 15%.
Sorted tally: uneven hem 9, zip ripples 7, wrong size 5, loose threads 3, iron shine or stain 2, skipped stitches 1. Check: 9 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 27.
Cumulative share: uneven hem 9 ÷ 27 = 33.3%; plus zips 16 ÷ 27 = 59.3%; plus wrong size 21 ÷ 27 = 77.8%.
Rework took about 25 minutes per faulty garment: 27 × 25 = 675 minutes, or 11.25 hours.
At her workroom cost of about ₦21.60 per minute (you will calculate yours in the next lesson), rework cost 675 × ₦21.60 = ₦14,580 in time alone, before any replaced fabric.
blocks.result: Three fault types cause 77.8% of the rework. Adaeze retrains one machinist on levelling hems, adds a first-piece check for zips, and makes the cut check include a second look at the measurement card. Her target for next month is a defect rate under 8%.

blocks.text: Quality is also safety and trust

A workroom that is scaling has more people, more machines and more extension cables, so safety habits must be written into the SOP, not left to memory. A workroom also holds clients' body measurements, phone numbers and fitting photos. Under the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, personal data should be collected for a clear purpose and kept secure. In practice: keep measurement books locked away, never post a client's photo without her permission, and do not share client lists in staff group chats.

blocks.title: Workroom safety checks to add to your SOP
blocks.text: Do not overload extension boxes with several machines and an iron; spread heavy loads and switch off at the wall at closing. Keep a working fire extinguisher suited to electrical fires near the door and keep exits clear of fabric rolls. Stand irons on their heel, never face down on fabric, and keep cords away from walkways. Change broken needles with the machine switched off, and keep a first aid box stocked.
Review the defect log with your team every week, not to blame people but to fix methods. When a fault is a method problem, update the operation sheet and the golden sample card so the fix lasts.

blocks.title: Pay for good pieces, not just pieces
blocks.text: If you pay any piece rate, count only pieces that pass the gate. Agree in writing that a worker reworks her own faults first, and track faults by operation, so training goes where it is needed.

takeaways: Check at four gates so faults are caught when they are cheap
Log every fault with fixed names and count your monthly defect rate
Sort faults with Pareto and fix the top few first
Rework has a real naira cost; safety and client privacy belong in the SOP too

activity.title: Run your defect log for two weeks
steps: Print or rule a defect log with the six columns from this lesson
Add the four gates to your SOP and job ticket
Log every fault for two weeks
Sort the tally into a Pareto table with cumulative percentages
Choose one fix for the top fault and test it
activity.evidence: Your completed defect log, Pareto table and a note of the fix you tried

lessons.title: The production costing sheet and monthly capacity: costing by the minute
objectives: Calculate your workroom's labour and overhead cost per productive minute
Build a costing sheet for a garment using fabric, trims and standard minutes
Set a price that protects a chosen margin
Calculate monthly capacity and capacity utilisation for a product mix

blocks.text: In a workroom with paid staff, the easiest way to cost labour and overhead fairly is **by the minute**. You already have standard minutes for each style from Module 1. Now you work out what one productive minute of your workroom costs, and multiply. This method also tells you how many garments your team can make in a month, which is the same calculation turned around.

blocks.name: spool-of-thread
blocks.caption: Thread, zips and interfacing are small costs, but on the costing sheet every one is listed.

blocks.text: Step 1: productive minutes in a month

Start with the paid minutes of all your sewing staff in a month. Then apply an **efficiency** figure: the share of paid time that turns into standard minutes of work. Nobody produces for every paid minute; there are machine stoppages, waiting, training and breaks. Measure your own efficiency by comparing standard minutes produced with paid minutes over a few weeks. A new workroom is often well below 100%.
Step 2: cost per productive minute

Divide monthly staff wages by productive minutes to get **labour cost per minute**. Divide monthly overheads by the same minutes to get **overhead cost per minute**. Overheads include rent, power and fuel, phone and data, machine servicing, and a fair salary for you as manager. Leaving your own salary out makes every price look profitable when it is not.

blocks.title: Worked example: Adaeze's cost per minute
blocks.context: Adaeze (for example) has three machinists. All naira figures are approximate and illustrative.
steps: Paid minutes: 24 days × 8 hours × 60 = 11,520 per person, so 3 × 11,520 = 34,560.
Measured efficiency 75%: 34,560 × 0.75 = 25,920 productive minutes.
Labour cost per minute: ₦255,000 ÷ 25,920 = about ₦9.84.
Overheads: rent ₦60,000, power and fuel ₦70,000, phone and data ₦10,000, servicing ₦15,000, her salary ₦150,000. Total ₦305,000. Overhead per minute: ₦305,000 ÷ 25,920 = about ₦11.77.
Together: ₦9.84 + ₦11.77 = ₦21.61, about ₦21.60 per productive minute.
blocks.result: Every standard minute a garment takes costs Adaeze about ₦21.60 in labour and overhead.

blocks.text: Step 3: the costing sheet

For fabric, use the yardage from your actual lay or marker, plus a waste allowance you have measured from your own offcuts. For trims, list every item. Then add labour and overhead from the SMV. Finally choose a margin. **Margin** is profit as a share of the selling price, so price = total cost ÷ (1 − margin). For a 40% margin, divide cost by 0.6.

Check one line yourself: for the dress, ₦7,920 + ₦1,400 + ₦738 + ₦883 = ₦10,941, and ₦10,941 ÷ 0.6 = ₦18,235. At ₦18,500 the margin is (₦18,500 − ₦10,941) ÷ ₦18,500, about 40.9%. When fabric prices change at the market, update the fabric line the same week.
Step 4: monthly capacity and utilisation

**Capacity** is productive minutes divided by SMV. If Adaeze made only shift dresses, capacity would be 25,920 ÷ 75 = about 345 dresses a month. Real months have a mix, so add up the standard minutes of your planned orders and compare with productive minutes. That share is **capacity utilisation**.

blocks.title: What a garment price is built from
items: Margin
Overhead minutes
Labour minutes
Trims
Fabric with waste
blocks.caption: Read from the base up: each layer is added on top of real costs, and margin comes last.

blocks.title: Worked example: will next month's orders fit?
blocks.context: Adaeze plans 120 shift dresses, 80 kaftans and 60 peplum tops.
steps: Dresses: 120 × 75 = 9,000 minutes.
Kaftans: 80 × 95 = 7,600 minutes.
Tops: 60 × 55 = 3,300 minutes.
Utilisation: 19,900 ÷ 25,920 = about 76.8%. Spare: 25,920 − 19,900 = 6,020 minutes.
blocks.result: The plan fits with 6,020 minutes spare, which leaves room for rework, fittings and one small extra order. She will not promise more than that without overtime or another worker.

blocks.title: Do not plan to 100%
blocks.text: Leave a buffer for rework, power cuts, sick days and late fabric. Treat any plan above about 85 to 90% of your productive minutes as a warning to add hours, delay a delivery date or decline an order.

takeaways: Cost labour and overhead by the productive minute
Include your own manager's salary in overheads
Price = total cost ÷ (1 − margin)
Capacity = productive minutes ÷ SMV; compare planned load to it every month

activity.title: Cost your three most-ordered garments
steps: Write your monthly wages, paid minutes and an efficiency estimate
Calculate labour and overhead cost per minute
Build a costing sheet for your three most-ordered garments
Set prices for a margin you choose and check each sum with a calculator
Add next month's planned orders and calculate utilisation
activity.evidence: Your costing sheet for three garments and a capacity calculation for next month

quiz.q: Adaeze's board shows 36 garments in progress and she finishes 4 a day. About how long does a garment spend in the workroom?
quiz.explain: Little's law: lead time = WIP ÷ throughput = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 days.

quiz.q: The Sew column has reached its WIP limit. What should the cutter do?
options: Cut the next three orders so they are ready
Stop cutting and help clear the Sew or Finish columns
quiz.explain: A full column means more cutting only builds piles. Helping downstream moves finished garments out faster.

quiz.q: Of 200 garments inspected, 16 had at least one fault. What is the defect rate?
Faults are hem 12, zips 6, size 4, threads 2. What cumulative percentage do the top two faults cover?
A garment costs ₦9,000 in total. What price gives a 40% margin?
quiz.explain: Price = cost ÷ (1 − 0.40) = ₦9,000 ÷ 0.6 = ₦15,000. Adding 40% to cost (₦12,600) gives a lower margin.

quiz.q: Productive minutes are 25,920 and next month's orders need 24,800 standard minutes. What is the best decision?
options: Accept more orders, there is still space
Treat it as nearly full (about 96%) and add hours or move a delivery date before accepting more
Ignore it, the team will manage
quiz.explain: 24,800 ÷ 25,920 is about 95.7%, leaving almost no buffer for rework or power cuts. She should add capacity or adjust dates first.

modules.title: Growing the Business: Channels, Team Pay and Your Scale-Up Plan
modules.overview: You test bulk, wholesale and contract offers against cost, cash and capacity, pay and lead a production team fairly, and pull every tool into a monthly dashboard, a buyer lookbook and a 90-day growth plan.

lessons.title: New channels at scale: boutique wholesale, consignment, uniform contracts and CMT terms
objectives: Compare outright wholesale with consignment for boutique sales
Test a bulk or credit order against your cost, cash and capacity
Write payment and delivery terms that protect your cash
Split a contract that is bigger than one month's spare capacity

blocks.text: Once your costs and capacity are known, you can grow through buyers who order many pieces at once: boutiques, schools, churches and mosques, companies, event planners and other fashion brands. These buyers bring volume, but they also ask for lower prices, longer payment times and firm deadlines. This lesson shows how to test each offer against three things you now measure: **cost, cash and capacity**.

blocks.name: contract
blocks.alt: Two people reviewing and signing a contract
blocks.caption: Bigger buyers need written terms: price, quantity, deposit, delivery and payment dates.

blocks.text: The four main channels

items: **Boutique wholesale**: a shop buys your ready-made pieces at a wholesale price and resells at its own retail price. You get volume and exposure; you give up part of the price.
**Consignment**: the boutique displays your pieces and pays you only for what sells, usually after an agreed period. Less selling effort for you, but your stock and cash wait on their shelf.
**Uniform and group contracts**: a school, company or religious group orders many pieces of one or a few styles in a size range, often with a fixed delivery date.
**CMT for other brands**: you cut, make and trim their fabric to their sample for a fee per piece.

blocks.title: Outright wholesale versus consignment
items: Outright wholesale
Consignment
left: You are paid on agreed date
Their risk if pieces don't sell
right: Often a higher share per piece
Your cash waits on their shelf
blocks.caption: Start new boutiques on a small consignment or a small outright order, then move good partners to larger outright orders.

blocks.text: Testing an offer: cost, cash, capacity

items: **Cost**: is the offered price above your total cost per piece from your costing sheet, with enough profit left?
**Cash**: how much do you spend before you are paid, and for how long? Can you pay wages and rent while you wait?
**Capacity**: do the standard minutes fit in your spare minutes this month without breaking promises to existing clients?

blocks.title: Worked example: a boutique wants 30 tops on 60-day credit
blocks.context: A boutique in Abuja (for example) offers Adaeze ₦11,000 each for 30 peplum tops, paying 60 days after delivery. Her costing sheet says each top costs ₦7,468.
steps: Cost: profit per top ₦11,000 − ₦7,468 = ₦3,532. For 30 tops: 30 × ₦3,532 = ₦105,960. The price works.
Cash: fabric and trims per top are ₦5,280 + ₦1,000 = ₦6,280, so she must spend 30 × ₦6,280 = ₦188,400 on materials before any payment, and wait 60 days after delivery for ₦330,000 (30 × ₦11,000).
Capacity: 30 × 55 = 1,650 minutes, well inside her 6,020 spare minutes.
Her counter-offer: same price, 50% deposit on order (₦165,000) and the balance on delivery, or 60-day terms on a first order of 10 pieces only.
blocks.result: The price and capacity are fine; cash is the problem. With a 50% deposit, ₦165,000 arrives before she buys ₦188,400 of materials, so she only funds ₦23,400 herself and is fully paid on delivery.

blocks.text: When the contract is bigger than your spare capacity

Big contracts are where workrooms most often fail, because the owner says yes before checking minutes. Use your standard minutes and productive minutes from Module 2, then choose: split delivery, add overtime that staff agree to, bring in a trusted partner workroom for some operations, or decline politely.

blocks.title: Worked example: 200 school pinafores
blocks.context: A private school (for example) asks Adaeze for 200 pinafores in one month. Her timed SMV for the pinafore is 40 minutes, and she has 6,020 spare minutes next month.
steps: Load: 200 × 40 = 8,000 minutes, which is 1,980 minutes more than her spare 6,020.
Option 1: deliver 150 in month one (150 × 40 = 6,000 minutes) and 50 at the start of month two (50 × 40 = 2,000 minutes).
Option 2: add agreed paid overtime or one temporary machinist trained on the two simplest operations.
She offers the school split delivery: the classes that start first get their pinafores first.
blocks.result: By checking minutes before saying yes, Adaeze gives the school a date she can keep, instead of promising 200 and delivering late.

blocks.text: Terms to put in writing

items: Style code, sample reference and size breakdown (for example 40 small, 90 medium, 70 large).
Price per piece, what it includes, and whether fabric is yours or theirs.
Deposit amount and date, balance due date, and how they pay, such as a bank transfer or a payment link from a provider like Paystack, Moniepoint or Opay.
Delivery dates, partial deliveries and who pays transport.
What happens to faulty pieces, late changes to the design, and spoiled fabric in CMT.
For consignment: the display period, your share of the selling price, how often they report sales, and when unsold pieces come back.

blocks.title: Check before you ship or pay
blocks.text: Confirm deposits in your own bank or payment app, not from a screenshot, before cutting. Scammers send fake transfer alerts and fake large orders that ask you to pay a fee first. Never pay a fee to receive an order.

blocks.title: Make a line sheet for buyers
blocks.text: A line sheet is a one-page list for trade buyers: photo, style code, sizes, colours, wholesale price, minimum order and lead time for each piece. It saves long WhatsApp chats and makes you look ready for business.

takeaways: Test every bulk or credit offer on cost, cash and capacity
Consignment keeps the risk with you; outright wholesale moves it to the buyer
Ask for a deposit that covers materials, or start partners small
Split or decline contracts that exceed your spare minutes

activity.title: Test one real or likely offer
steps: Choose one buyer type you could approach in the next three months
Write a realistic order: quantity, style, price and payment terms
Test it on cost, cash and capacity using your costing sheet
Write your counter-offer terms
Draft a one-page line sheet for three pieces
activity.evidence: Your offer test calculations, written terms and the line sheet

lessons.title: Paying and leading a production team: salary, piece rate from standard minutes and written agreements
objectives: Compare salary, piece rate and blended pay for workroom staff
Calculate a fair piece rate from standard minutes and a target day's pay
Write the key points of a workroom staff agreement
Run a short daily huddle and a weekly review

blocks.text: Growing past three or four people changes the owner's job. You spend less time sewing and more time planning, training, checking and paying. Most conflict in Nigerian workrooms comes from things that were never written down: how pay is calculated, who pays for spoiled fabric, what hours are expected in December rush. Decide these before you hire, and write them down.

blocks.name: team-goals
blocks.alt: A small team gathered around a shared goal
blocks.caption: Clear pay rules and shared targets keep a growing team working together.

blocks.text: Three ways to pay

blocks.title: Monthly salary versus piece rate
items: Monthly salary
Piece rate
left: Easier to move people between tasks
right: Workers may rush and cut quality
blocks.caption: A blended system, a base salary plus a bonus per good piece above a target, combines the strengths of both.

blocks.text: Piecework is common in garment production worldwide, and it has a known weakness: if the rate per piece is too low, workers must go faster to earn a living, and quality suffers. That is why the rate must be built from timed standard minutes, and why only pieces that pass the quality gate are paid.
Building a fair piece rate

items: Choose a target day's pay that a trained worker at a normal, steady pace should earn. Make sure it is never below the current national minimum wage when worked out for a month; check the current figure with the Ministry of Labour or a trusted news source, because it changes.
Take the standard minutes of the operation from your operation sheet.
Work out pieces per day at 100% pace: paid minutes per day ÷ standard minutes.
Adjust to an expected pace using your measured efficiency, so an average worker can reach the target.
Piece rate = target day's pay ÷ expected pieces per day.

blocks.title: Worked example: the side-seam-and-hem operation
blocks.context: Adaeze (for example) wants to pay one machinist per piece for closing side seams and hemming peplum tops. The timed standard is 12 minutes. Her target pay for a trained worker is ₦3,600 for an 8-hour day (illustrative).
steps: Pieces per day at 100% pace: 480 ÷ 12 = 40.
Expected pace using her measured 75% efficiency: 40 × 0.75 = 30 pieces.
Piece rate: ₦3,600 ÷ 30 = ₦120 per good piece.
A fast, careful worker at 90%: 36 pieces × ₦120 = ₦4,320 a day. A slower learner at 60%: 24 × ₦120 = ₦2,880, so she keeps the learner on base pay plus training until she reaches the expected pace.
blocks.result: The rate is fair because an average trained worker reaches the target, faster workers earn more, and pay is only for pieces that pass inspection.

blocks.text: Blended pay: a base plus a quality bonus

Many growing workrooms settle on a blend. Each worker gets a fixed monthly base that covers her basic needs and keeps her steady in slow months, plus a small bonus for each good piece above a monthly target. The base protects the worker; the bonus rewards output; the quality gate protects the client. Set the target from your standard minutes so that an average trained worker can pass it in a normal month.

items: Example of a blended rule (illustrative): base ₦60,000 a month, plus ₦60 for every good piece above 600 good pieces in the month.
A worker who makes 780 good pieces earns a bonus of (780 − 600) × ₦60 = ₦10,800, so ₦60,000 + ₦10,800 = ₦70,800 for the month.
A worker who makes 550 good pieces earns the base of ₦60,000 and gets coaching on her slowest operation, not a deduction.

blocks.text: When a worker is below standard for several weeks, look first at the method and the machine, then at training, and only then at the person. Ask her to show you the operation, compare with the golden sample and the time standard, and agree one change to try for a week. Write down what was agreed. Most underperformance in a workroom comes from unclear instructions, poorly maintained machines or constant switching between tasks, which the owner can fix.
What the written agreement should cover

items: Role and main operations, and who she reports to.
Pay method, rate or salary, pay day and how pieces are counted.
Working hours, breaks, and how overtime is agreed and paid.
Trial period and how training is recognised.
Spoiled fabric: agree a cap on any deduction in writing, and never deduct for faults caused by someone else or by unclear instructions.
Care of machines and tools, safety rules, and client privacy: no photos of client garments or measurement books on personal social media.
Notice period on both sides.

blocks.text: For legal questions, such as contracts or tax and pension duties once you employ more people, ask a lawyer or an accountant. This course does not give legal advice.

blocks.title: Apprentices are not free labour
blocks.text: If you train apprentices, write down what they will learn, by when, any stipend, and their hours. Use your operation list and training wall chart as their learning plan, and sign off each operation as they master it.
Leading the day: the huddle and the weekly review

Hold a 10-minute **daily huddle** at the job board before machines start: what is due today, which column is full, who covers which operation, any quality fault from yesterday. Once a week, take 30 minutes for a **review**: delivered on time, defect log top fault, any safety issue, and one improvement to try. Thank people by name for specific work. A team that sees the numbers understands why WIP limits and quality gates matter.

blocks.title: Cross-train for cover
blocks.text: Use your training wall chart to make sure every operation has at least two people signed off. When one machinist is sick during a wedding rush, the line keeps moving.

takeaways: Choose salary, piece rate or blended pay deliberately and write it down
Build piece rates from standard minutes, a target day's pay and expected pace
Pay only for pieces that pass inspection, and cap fabric deductions in writing
Lead with a daily huddle at the board and a weekly review of the numbers

activity.title: Design your pay and agreement
steps: Pick one operation with a timed standard
Calculate a piece rate from a target day's pay and your efficiency
Check what fast, average and learner workers would earn
Draft a one-page staff agreement with the points from this lesson
Run one daily huddle and note what came up
activity.evidence: Your piece-rate calculation, the draft agreement and huddle notes

lessons.title: Your scale-up dashboard, buyer lookbook and 90-day growth plan
objectives: Track five operations numbers on a monthly dashboard
Prepare a trade lookbook and line sheet for buyers
Calculate what adding one machinist does to capacity and cost per minute
Write a 90-day growth plan with targets and owners

blocks.text: You now have the tools of a production manager: time audit, model mix, operation sheets, job board, quality gates, minute costing, channel tests and fair pay. This final lesson ties them into a **monthly dashboard** that shows whether the business is really scaling, a **buyer-facing portfolio** to bring the right volume in, and a **90-day plan** that turns it all into actions.

blocks.name: growth-analytics
blocks.alt: A person reviewing growth charts on a dashboard
blocks.caption: A one-page dashboard shows whether more orders are turning into better delivery, quality and margin.

blocks.text: The five numbers on your dashboard

head: Number
How to calculate
Where it comes from
rows: Garments delivered by the promised date ÷ all garments delivered
Garments with a fault at inspection ÷ garments inspected
Standard minutes produced ÷ productive minutes available
Average work in progress ÷ garments finished per day
(Price − total cost) ÷ price, for your top three styles

blocks.title: Worked example: Adaeze's dashboard after one month
blocks.context: Adaeze (for example) fills her dashboard at month end.
steps: On time: 187 of 210 garments delivered by the promised date. 187 ÷ 210 = about 89.0%.
Defect rate: 16 faulty out of 200 inspected = 8%, down from 15% the month before.
Utilisation: 19,900 standard minutes ÷ 25,920 productive minutes = about 76.8%.
Lead time: average WIP 20 ÷ 4 finished per day = 5 days, down from 9.
Margins: shift dress about 40.9%, peplum top about 40.3%, kaftan about 40.1%.
blocks.result: Quality and lead time improved, but 23 late garments (210 − 187) are still too many. Her next target is 95% on time, which means tighter due-date setting at intake.

blocks.text: Reading the dashboard

Look at the numbers together, not one at a time. Rising utilisation with a rising defect rate usually means the team is rushing; slow down intake before quality damages your name. Long lead time with low utilisation usually means work is stuck at one stage, often waiting for cutting or for client fittings, so check the job board for the full column. Falling margin on a style with steady prices usually means fabric has gone up at the market or the style is taking longer than its standard; re-time it and update the costing sheet. Write one sentence under the dashboard each month: what the numbers say and the one thing you will change.

Keep the dashboard on one page and keep every month's copy in a file or a phone folder. After three months you can see a trend, which matters more than any single month, because one big wedding order or one power-cut week can distort a month's figures.
Portfolio for buyers, not just for likes

For individual clients, a WhatsApp Business catalogue and Instagram posts work. Trade buyers need something different: proof you can repeat a style in volume to a standard. Build a short **trade lookbook** of 8 to 12 pages: your best styles photographed on a model or mannequin in good daylight, a photo of your job board and inspection table, your size chart, and a **line sheet** with style codes, sizes, wholesale prices, minimum order and lead time. Get written permission before using any client's photo.
Planning the next step up: adding a machinist

blocks.title: Worked example: what a fourth machinist changes
blocks.context: Adaeze considers hiring a fourth machinist at ₦85,000 a month (illustrative), keeping overheads at ₦305,000.
steps: Productive minutes: 4 × 11,520 × 0.75 = 34,560, up from 25,920.
Shift dress capacity: 34,560 ÷ 75 = about 460 a month, up from about 345.
But the lower cost per minute only holds if the extra minutes are sold. At today's load of 19,900 minutes, utilisation would fall to 19,900 ÷ 34,560 = about 57.6%.
blocks.result: Adaeze will hire once she has signed contracts or steady orders that push her current utilisation above about 85% for two months in a row. Until then she fills gaps with CMT work.

blocks.title: A 90-day scale-up plan
items: Days 1-30: measure and standardise
Days 31-60: systems and pricing
Days 61-90: new channel and team
blocks.caption: Each month builds on the last: you cannot price or sell volume well until your standard and numbers are in place.

blocks.text: Writing your 90-day plan

items: Write your current five dashboard numbers as the starting point.
Choose your target model mix and target monthly capacity in standard minutes.

For each 30-day block, write three actions with an owner and a due date, for example: train Chioma to sign-off on cutting by day 25; set WIP limits and post the SOP by day 35; send line sheet to three boutiques by day 70.
Set end-of-plan targets, for example on-time delivery 95%, defect rate under 6%, utilisation 80 to 85%.
Book a review date on day 30, 60 and 90, and update the plan, not just the numbers.

blocks.title: Grow at the speed of your systems
blocks.text: If on-time delivery or defect rate gets worse while orders rise, pause new channels and fix the system first. Growth that damages your name with clients is not growth.

takeaways: Track on-time delivery, defect rate, utilisation, lead time and margin every month
Trade buyers want proof of repeatable quality: a lookbook and line sheet
Extra staff lower cost per minute only when the extra minutes are sold
A 90-day plan needs actions, owners, dates and review points

activity.title: Build your dashboard and 90-day plan
steps: Calculate your five dashboard numbers for last month
Draft an 8 to 12 page trade lookbook outline and one line sheet
Test what one extra worker would do to capacity and cost per minute
Write your 90-day plan with three actions per month
Share it with your team in a huddle
activity.evidence: Your dashboard, lookbook outline, line sheet and signed 90-day plan

quiz.q: A boutique offers ₦11,000 per top on 60-day credit. Cost per top is ₦7,468 and materials per top are ₦6,280. What is the main problem with 30 tops?
options: Cash: about ₦188,400 of materials must be paid long before any payment arrives
The profit per top is negative
quiz.explain: Price and capacity work. The risk is cash: 30 × ₦6,280 = ₦188,400 spent up front with payment 60 days after delivery.

quiz.q: Which arrangement keeps the stock risk with the maker?
options: A uniform contract with a deposit
quiz.explain: In consignment you still own the pieces and are paid only when they sell.

quiz.q: A contract needs 200 × 40 = 8,000 standard minutes and you have 6,020 spare. What is a sound response?
options: Accept and hope the team works faster
Offer split delivery or add agreed capacity before accepting
quiz.explain: The load is 1,980 minutes over spare capacity. Splitting delivery or adding capacity keeps the promise realistic.

quiz.q: An operation has a standard of 10 minutes. Paid day is 480 minutes, efficiency 75%, target day's pay ₦3,600. What is the piece rate?
quiz.explain: 480 ÷ 10 = 48 at 100% pace; 48 × 0.75 = 36 expected pieces; ₦3,600 ÷ 36 = ₦100 per good piece.

quiz.q: Why should piece rates count only pieces that pass inspection?
options: Because piece rates can push workers to rush and cut quality
Because it is easier to count
quiz.explain: Paying only for good pieces keeps the speed incentive from damaging quality.

quiz.q: 187 of 210 garments were delivered on time. What is the on-time delivery rate?

finalQuiz.q: Which task is usually the best first one to hand to a trained helper?
options: Alterations and overlocking, which are low value per owner hour and transferable
finalQuiz.explain: Low-value, transferable work frees owner hours for the work only she can do yet.

finalQuiz.q: A made-to-measure dress sells for ₦38,000, uses ₦14,000 of materials and takes 4 hours. What is contribution per workroom hour?
In CMT work, who normally supplies the main fabric?
finalQuiz.explain: In cut, make, trim work the brand supplies fabric and a sample; the workroom is paid a fee per piece.

finalQuiz.q: Observed time 12 minutes, rating 100%, allowance 15%. What is the standard time?
When should a helper be signed off on an operation?
options: After three pieces in a row match the golden sample within the time standard
After one week, whatever the result
When she says she is ready
finalQuiz.explain: Sign-off is based on evidence: consistent pieces that match the sample at a reasonable time.

finalQuiz.q: A workroom has 30 garments in progress and wants a 5-day lead time. How many must it finish per day?
finalQuiz.explain: Throughput = WIP ÷ lead time = 30 ÷ 5 = 6 garments per day.

finalQuiz.q: Where is a cutting error cheapest to catch?
options: When the client tries the garment on
At the cut check, before sewing
At the first-piece check of the hem
finalQuiz.explain: The cut check comes before any sewing, so a fault found there costs minutes rather than fabric and hours.

finalQuiz.q: Rework took 40 garments × 20 minutes, and the workroom costs ₦21.60 per minute. What did rework cost in time?
Wages are ₦255,000 and overheads ₦305,000 for 25,920 productive minutes. Why must the owner's salary be in overheads?
options: Without it every price looks profitable while the owner works unpaid
finalQuiz.explain: Leaving the manager's salary out hides a real cost, so prices seem fine while the business does not pay its owner.

finalQuiz.q: Productive minutes are 25,920 and a style has an SMV of 60. What is the monthly capacity for that style alone?
A new boutique asks for 40 pieces on 90-day credit. What is a sensible first step?
options: Accept all terms to win the account
Offer a small first order or consignment, or ask a deposit that covers materials
Lower your price below cost to impress them
finalQuiz.explain: Starting small or with a deposit protects cash while you test the partner.

finalQuiz.q: Adding a machinist lowers cost per minute on paper. When is that true in practice?
options: Only when the extra minutes are filled with sold work
Only if the new worker is paid by the piece
finalQuiz.explain: Idle minutes still cost wages. The lower cost per minute appears only when utilisation stays high.

capstone.title: Fashion Business Scale-Up Project
capstone.brief: Produce a scale-up pack for your own workroom: a minute-based costing sheet for your three most-ordered garments, a one-page workflow SOP from intake to delivery with quality checkpoints marked, and a 90-day growth plan naming your business model mix, target monthly capacity and next concrete actions.
steps: Complete a two-week time log and order-mix review and name your constraint
Write operation sheets with timed standard minutes for your three most-ordered garments
Calculate your labour and overhead cost per productive minute
Build the costing sheet for the three garments (fabric with waste, trims, labour, overhead, margin) and check every sum
Write and post your one-page SOP with stage owners, WIP limits and the four quality gates starred
Fill in your five-number dashboard for one month
Write your 90-day plan with model mix, target capacity in standard minutes, three actions per month, owners and review dates
evidence: Costing sheet for three garments with all sums checked
Signed one-page SOP with quality checkpoints marked
Photo of your job board and a completed defect log
90-day growth plan with model mix and target capacity
